## The problem

Some tools are not programs you run but services you connect to:
JupyterLab, RStudio Server, VS Code's server, TensorBoard, a Dask dashboard.
They listen on a port, and you use them from a browser or an editor on your laptop.
On an HPC you want them on a compute node, not on the shared login node,
which leaves a path with one missing piece:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  laptop["laptop"]
  login["login node"]
  compute["compute node"]
  laptop -- "ssh" --> login
  login -. "???" .-> compute
```

You can SSH to the login node, but normally not onward to a compute node,
so something has to carry the connection across that last hop.
The recipe you will most often find is to make the app listen on the compute node's network address and tunnel to it
([method 1a](30-plain-http.md)).
That works, but it leaves your app, and whatever you type into it, open to everyone else on the cluster.
Keep in mind that a Jupyter or RStudio session is a way to run any code as you,
so whoever gets into it gets your account.

All the methods here run without any help from the admins.
If your facility offers something like [Open OnDemand](https://openondemand.org/),
which is built to solve exactly this, use that instead.

## The methods

If what you want runs in a terminal, you don't need any of this:
[method 0](20-shell.md) is just a shell on the compute node.
For everything with a port, the methods fall into three groups,
by *where the app listens* and *how your laptop gets to it*.

### Group 1: the app listens on the cluster network

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  laptop["laptop"]
  login["login node"]
  app["app on the compute node<br/>(cluster network address)"]
  other["anyone else on the cluster"]
  laptop -- "ssh -L (encrypted)" --> login
  login -- "1a: HTTP, unencrypted<br/>1b: HTTPS, encrypted" --> app
  other -. "can connect too" .-> app
```

[1a](30-plain-http.md) is the usual recipe, in plain HTTP.
[1b](40-tls.md) is the same with HTTPS, so nobody can read your token off the network any more.
In both, anyone on the cluster can still connect to the port, so the app's own token is what keeps them out.

### Group 2: SSH over Slurm

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  laptop["laptop"]
  login["login node"]
  sshd["sshd -i<br/>(on the compute node)"]
  app["app on 127.0.0.1"]
  laptop -- "ssh" --> login
  login -- "srun" --> sshd
  sshd -- "ssh -L" --> app
```

The app listens only on the compute node's loopback, which nothing else on the cluster can reach.
[Method 2](50-srun-ssh.qmd) runs an SSH server over `srun`,
so your laptop gets one SSH session that reaches all the way to the app.

### Group 3: the job connects out to a relay

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  laptop["laptop"]
  relay["relay<br/>3a: your server<br/>3b: Microsoft Dev Tunnels<br/>3c: Cloudflare"]
  app["app on 127.0.0.1"]
  app -- "outbound connection" --> relay
  laptop -- "ssh or https" --> relay
```

The app again listens only on loopback, and the job connects *out* to a relay that your laptop can also reach.
They differ in who runs the relay:
you ([3a](60-own-relay.qmd)), Microsoft ([3b](70-dev-tunnel.md)), or Cloudflare ([3c](80-cloudflare-tunnel.md)).

## Comparison

| Method | App listens on | Encrypted all the way | Who can connect to the app | Third party | Needs |
|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| [0](20-shell.md) shell | (no port) | yes (SSH + Slurm) | nobody | none | Slurm |
| [1a](30-plain-http.md) HTTP | cluster network | **no** | **anyone on the cluster** | none | Slurm |
| [1b](40-tls.md) HTTPS | cluster network | yes | anyone on the cluster, stopped by the token | none | Slurm, `openssl` |
| [2](50-srun-ssh.qmd) SSH over srun | loopback | yes | only you | none | Slurm, an `sshd` binary |
| [3a](60-own-relay.qmd) own relay | loopback | yes | only you | your server | outbound SSH, a server |
| [3b](70-dev-tunnel.md) Dev Tunnels | loopback | yes, to the relay | only your account | Microsoft | outbound internet, GitHub/Microsoft account |
| [3c](80-cloudflare-tunnel.md) Cloudflare | loopback | yes, to the relay | **anyone with the URL**, stopped by the token | Cloudflare | outbound internet |

And what each is like to use:

| Method | One-off setup | Each time, on the cluster | Each time, on the laptop | Browser warning |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| [1b](40-tls.md) HTTPS | none | `sbatch launch.sh` | `connect.sh`, open URL | yes, self-signed certificate |
| [2](50-srun-ssh.qmd) SSH over srun | none | `sbatch launch.sh` | `connect.sh`, open URL | no |
| [3a](60-own-relay.qmd) own relay | a server and a key | `sbatch launch.sh` | `connect.sh`, open URL | no |
| [3b](70-dev-tunnel.md) Dev Tunnels | `setup.sh` (sign in) | `sbatch launch.sh` | `connect.sh` opens it; sign in | once per tunnel |
| [3c](80-cloudflare-tunnel.md) Cloudflare | none | `sbatch launch.sh` | `connect.sh` opens it | no |

## Which one

- **[Method 2](50-srun-ssh.qmd)**, if your cluster lets you run `sshd` (most do).
  Nothing listens on the cluster network, SSH does the rest, and nobody else is involved.
- **[Method 1b](40-tls.md)**, if you want the smallest change from what you do now.
  Still `ssh -L` and a URL, but encrypted.
- **[Method 3b](70-dev-tunnel.md)**, if you would rather not handle tunnels at all and don't mind Microsoft in the path,
  especially if your cluster already sends you to `code tunnel` for VS Code.
- **[Method 3a](60-own-relay.qmd)**, if you happen to have a server and want everything under your control.
- **[Method 3c](80-cloudflare-tunnel.md)**, only for a quick look, with a strong token.
- **Not [method 1a](30-plain-http.md).**

## Using the examples

Every method comes with scripts that work as they are, serving a small demo app in place of Jupyter and friends.
They are in [this guide's repository](https://github.com/ickc/hpc.kolen.dev) under `src/interactive-apps/examples`,
so the easiest way to get them is to clone it on the cluster and, for the laptop side, on your laptop.
Each method's page shows its scripts in full and says where to put your own app.

They assume as little as possible about your cluster, and each page lists what it does assume.
Common to all of them:

- **Slurm.** You submit jobs with `sbatch` and run things in them with `srun`.
- **Your cluster's options are yours to add.** Nothing in the scripts names an account, partition or QoS.
  Pass them as usual (`sbatch -A myproject -p mypartition launch.sh`),
  or set them once in the environment:
  `SBATCH_ACCOUNT` and `SBATCH_PARTITION` for `sbatch`, `SLURM_ACCOUNT` and `SLURM_PARTITION` for `srun`.
- **A shared home directory.** The job writes what the laptop side needs (ports, keys, URLs) to
  `~/.interactive-apps/<JOBID>`, readable only by you, and the laptop side reads it from the login node.
- **`LOGIN_HOST`** is whatever you type after `ssh` to reach the login node, e.g. an alias from your `~/.ssh/config`.
- **Submit from the example's directory**, since the job finds the demo app relative to it.

## Testing the examples

Each example has a `test.sh` that runs on a login node, submits the real job, connects the way your laptop would,
and checks the demo page comes back.
The one hop it cannot do from the login node is laptop to login node, which is your ordinary SSH login.
The tests are necessarily a little different for each method; each page says what its test does.

Run them all, in parallel, with

``` bash
./run-tests.sh                 # or: ./run-tests.sh srun-ssh tls
```

from the `examples` directory (or `pixi run test-examples` from the top of the repository).
A test passes, fails, or is skipped when something it needs is missing,
e.g. a relay for 3a or a signed-in `devtunnel` for 3b.
Each test cancels its jobs when it finishes, and gives up if its job has not started within
`QUEUE_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 900).
